Emulating DGEMM and ZGEMM with INT8 Matrix Engines on Intel Arc GPUs: Ozaki Scheme II on the Xe2 Architecture

**Abstract**

Double-precision matrix multiplication, real (DGEMM) and complex (ZGEMM), dominates the run time of dense linear algebra and electronic-structure codes. On affordable GPUs, however, FP64 throughput is a small and shrinking fraction of the throughput of the low-precision matrix engines. Ozaki scheme II closes this gap by reducing a floating-point matrix product to a handful of exact INT8 products followed by a Chinese-remainder reconstruction; the number of products sets the accuracy. We present what is, to our knowledge, the first implementation of Ozaki scheme II for Intel GPUs. Written in SYCL on top of oneMKL, it runs entirely on the device and exposes the full BLAS `dgemm/zgemm` interface, including transposition, conjugation, \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and arbitrary problem sizes through memory- aware tiling. Making the scheme fast on the Xe2 (Battlemage) architecture required keeping FP64 arithmetic out of all memory-bound kernels, a branch-free residue computation, an FP32 evaluation of the CRT quotient with a proven safety margin, 16-bit limb arithmetic in the reconstruction, and work-arounds for performance cliffs of the vendor INT8 GEMM. On an Intel Arc Pro B60 (24GB) the emulated DGEMM reaches 17.3, 12.1 and 9.3 TFLOP/s with _s_=8, 12 and 16 moduli at _N_=8192, and up to 21.1 TFLOP/s overall, i.e. 12-28\(\times\) the native FP64 DGEMM of the same board; 75-90% of the run time is spent in INT8 GEMM at ≈95% of its attainable rate. The emulated ZGEMM, which uses the 3M form exactly in integer arithmetic, reaches up to 27.4 TFLOP/s and is 13.7-17.8\(\times\) faster than native ZGEMM for \(N\ge 4096\) at _s_=16. With \(s\ge 16\) the results are correctly rounded for well-scaled inputs and, using an extended-width residue path (_s_=20-24), also for inputs with wide exponent ranges, whereas native DGEMM on GPU or CPU rounds only 2-13% of the entries correctly. We further report worst-case accuracy, phase breakdowns, energy, an ablation of the pipeline-level decisions, a comparison with Ozaki scheme I on the same hardware, and a validated performance model for projecting the method to Intel’s announced Xe3P-based products.

## 1 Introduction

High-precision matrix multiplication. The general matrix product \(C ←\alpha\mathrm{op}(A)\mathrm{op}(B)+\beta C\) (GEMM, a level-3 BLAS routine [1]) is the kernel onto which dense linear algebra is mapped: blocked LU, Cholesky and QR factorizations, eigenvalue and singular-value solvers, and the High-Performance LINPACK benchmark all perform the overwhelming majority of their floating- point operations in GEMM [2]. Computational chemistry and materials science are a prominent example: self-consistent-field methods such as Hartree–Fock and Kohn–Sham density functional

<tbc>theory repeatedly transform and multiply dense Fock, overlap and density matrices, both in localized-basis and in plane-wave implementations (e.g. \[3\]). With Bloch _k_-points these matrices are complex Hermitian, and many-body perturbation methods such as GW \[4\] are dominated by large complex products (ZGEMM). Complex GEMM is equally central to frequency-domain electromagnetics, quantum transport and quantum-circuit simulation.

These applications need double precision. Total-energy differences of a few meV on totals of 10<sup>3</sup>-10<sup>5</sup>Hartree, orbital orthogonalization, ill-conditioned overlap matrices and long iterative processes all amplify rounding errors beyond what single precision can absorb \[5\]. Mixed- precision algorithms such as iterative refinement move part of the work to lower precision \[6, 7\], but they still require an FP64 residual and do not replace GEMM itself.

## The FP64 gap and its emulation.

GPU vendors now spend most of their transistor budget on low-precision matrix engines for machine learning, and FP64 is falling behind. On NVIDIA’s current Blackwell generation, both the GeForce RTX 50 series and the RTX PRO workstation boards built on the same GB20x chips execute FP64 at 1/64 of the FP32 rate \[8\]. Even in the data centre, the Blackwell Ultra platform HGX B300 delivers 10 TFFLOP/s of FP64, compared with 296 TFFLOP/s for its predecessor HGX B200 \[9\]. Emulating FP64 GEMM with exact low-precision products is therefore attractive, and NVIDIA itself now ships such an emulation in cuBLAS \[10, 11\]. Ozaki scheme I \[12\] splits the significands into _L_ slices and needs _O(L_<sup>2</sup>) slice products; it has been mapped to Tensor Cores \[13\] and to INT8 engines \[14, 15\], and a related splitting recovers FP32 accuracy on Tensor Cores \[16\]. Ozaki scheme II \[17\] takes a different route. Instead of splitting the significands, it represents the integrated matrices by their residues modulo _s_ small, pairwise coprime integers and multiplies the residue matrices exactly. Each additional modulus adds about 8 bits of precision at the cost of one more INT8 product, so the work grows linearly rather than quadratically with the target precision. The scheme has since been extended to FP8 \[18\] and to complex products \[19\], and shown to be competitive on CPUs with AMX and SVE2 \[20\].

## Why Intel Arc.

Intel’s Xe2-based Arc Pro B60 offers 24GB of GDDR6 \[21\] at a retail price of about US$600 \[22\], an unusually large memory for its price class. Unlike the preceding Arc Alchemist generation, Xe2 has native FP64 support \[23\], but only at 1/16 of the FP32 rate: we measure 0.76 TFFLOP/s for DGEMM and 11.9 TFFLOP/s for SGEMM, while the XMX matrix engines deliver ≈190TOP/s of INT8. This ratio of ≈250 between INT8 and FP64 throughput lets the emulation pay off by an order of magnitude, and the large memory accommodates the _O(sN_<sup>2</sup>) workspace of the scheme for large problems. Intel has also announced, but not yet shipped, its Xe3P-based data-centre GPU "Crescent Island" \[24\], now the Intel GPU D- Series. Its first model, the D270, carries up to 480GB of LPDDR5X and is advertised for workloads from low-precision inference to FP64 scientific computing \[25\]. Both products thus combine large memory with strong low-precision throughput, which makes them natural targets for Ozaki scheme II.

## Contributions.

• A complete, device-resident DGEMM/ZGEMM emulation for Intel GPUs in SYCL and oneMKL, with the full BLAS interface (`N/T/C`, \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), leading dimensions), \(2\le s\le 24\) moduli, memory-aware tiling and _k_-splitting (Sections 4 and 5).<tbc>

• The implementation choices that matter on Xe2: integer-only residue generation from the bits of IEEE doubles, a branch-free symmetric residue, an FP32 CRT quotient with a proven safety margin of 1/4, 16-bit limb accumulation, correctly rounded conversion, and work-arounds for performance cliffs of the oneMKL INT8 GEMM and for VRAM over-subscription (Section 6).<tbc>

• A ZGEMM in the exact 3M (Karatsuba) form of \[19\], integrated into the same device- resident pipeline: the split kernel emits the residues of _A<sub>r</sub>+A<sub>i</sub>_ directly, and the CRT kernel combines the three products before reconstruction, so that a complex product costs 3_s_ INT8 GEMMs and inherits the accuracy of the real case (Section 5).<tbc>

• An extended-width residue path (scaling width _t_ up to 100 bits) that delivers correctly rounded DGEMM and ZGEMM for inputs with wide exponent ranges.<tbc>

• A systematic evaluation covering verification (unit tests of the kernels and element-wise checks of the error bound), accuracy against a double-double reference for typical and worst-case inputs, performance with a breakdown into phases, energy efficiency, an ablation study, a comparison with Ozaki scheme I on the same INT8 engine, and a validated performance model (Sections 7-9).

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Notation

We write \(\mathrm{op}(A)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times k}\) and \(\mathrm{op}(B)\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}\), stored in column-major order, and _u_=2<sup>-53</sup>. For an integer _x_ and a modulus _m_, sym_<sub>m</sub>(x_) denotes the representative of _x_mod_m_ in a fixed window of _m_ consecutive integers that contains 0; for \(m\le 256\) it fits in a signed byte. rint denotes rounding to nearest with ties to even.

### 2.2 Ozaki scheme I

Ozaki scheme I \[12\] writes each scaled row of _A_ and column of _B_ as a sum of _L_ low-precision slices, \(A\approx\sum_iA_i\) and \(B\approx\sum_jB_j\), chosen so that a low-precision engine computes every product _A<sub>i</sub>B<sub>j</sub>_ without rounding. The approximation \(AB\approx\sum_{i+j\le L+1}A_iB_j\) then requires _L(L_+1)/2 products. The INT8 variants \[14, 15\] use slices of about 7 bits.

### 2.3 Ozaki scheme II

Ozaki scheme II \[17\] consists of four steps. We follow the formulation of the original paper, with the modifications described in Section 4.

_1. Integration with shared exponents._ Each row _i_ of _A_ and each column _j_ of _B_ is scaled by a power of two such that

\(\hat{a}_{ip}=\mathrm{rint}(a_{ip}2^{D_i}),\hat{b}_{pj}=\mathrm{rint}(b_{pj}2^{E_j}),|\hat{a}_{ip}|,|\hat{b}_{pj}|\le 2^t.\) (1)

Then \(\hat{c}_{ij}=\sum_p\hat{a}_{ip}\hat{b}_{pj}\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(c_{ij}\approx 2^{-D_i-E_j}\hat{c}_{ij}\). Errors arise only from the rounding in Eq. (1) and from the final rounding of \(\hat{c}_{ij}2^{-D_i-E_j}\).

_2. Residues._ For pairwise coprime moduli \(m_1,\dots,m_s\le 256\) with \(M=\prod_tm_t\), the residue matrices \(A^{(t)}=\mathrm{sym}_{m_t}(\hat{A})\) and \(B^{(t)}=\mathrm{sym}_{m_t}(\hat{B})\) have entries in \[-128,128\] and are stored as INT8.

_3. Exact INT8 products._ Each product _C_<sup>(_t_)</sup>=_A_<sup>(_t_)</sup>_B_<sup>(_t_)</sup> is computed with INT32 accumulation and is exact as long as \(k\cdot 128^2<2^{31}\), i.e. \(k\le 131071\).

_4. CRT reconstruction._ By the Chinese remainder theorem (see, e.g., \[26, §4.3.2\]), with _M<sub>t</sub>=M/m<sub>t</sub>_ and \(y_t=M_t^{-1}\mathrm{mod}m_t\),

\(\hat{c}_{ij}\equiv\sum_{t=1}^sC_{ij}^{(t)}M_ty_t(\mathrm{mod}M),\) (2)

and \(\hat{c}_{ij}\) is the unique representative with \(|\hat{c}_{ij}|<M/2\), provided that \(|\hat{c}_{ij}|<M/2\) is known a priori. The method needs _s_ INT8 products, and each modulus contributes log<sub>2</sub>_m<sub>t</sub>_≈7.9 bits to log<sub>2</sub>_M_.

### 2.4 Related implementations

GEMMul8 \[27\] implements Ozaki scheme II for NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and ozIMMU \[28\] implements the INT8 variant of Ozaki scheme I. Kouya \[20\] implements Ozaki scheme II for multiple precision on Intel AMX and Arm SVE2. Uchino et al. \[19\] extend Ozaki scheme II to CGEMM and ZGEMM with a Karatsuba (3M) formulation, also released in GEMMul8, and report speed-ups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. Among vendor libraries, cuBLAS has offered opt-in fixed-point emulation of FP64 matrix products (DGEMM and ZGEMM) on INT8 Tensor Cores since CUDA 13.0 Update 2 \[10, 11\], whereas the oneMKL 2026 release notes list no comparable feature \[29\]. We are not aware of any implementation for Intel GPUs.

## 3 Target platform: Intel Arc Pro B60 (Xe2)

The B60 has 20 Xe2 cores with 160 XMX matrix engines and 24 GB of GDDR6 on a 192-bit bus with a nominal bandwidth of 456 GB/s. Intel specifies 197TOP/s of dense INT8, 12.28 TFLOP/s of FP32 and a total board power of 120-200W, depending on the partner design \[21\]; the maximum GPU clock of our board is 2.4GHz.  1 lists the measured throughput of the operations relevant here. Three properties of the device shape the implementation:

(i) INT8 GEMM in oneMKL reaches 184-186TOP/s, about 250 times the native DGEMM rate of 0.76 TFLOP/s.<tbc>

(ii) FP64 vector arithmetic runs at 1/16 of the FP32 rate, and the conversion from FP64 to INT64 is not native. Kernels that are meant to run at memory speed must therefore avoid FP64 altogether.<tbc>

(iii) The memory bandwidth is ≈400GB/s for incompressible data, but the hardware compresses regular data (constant buffers are read at 1.1TB/s). All memory-bound measurements therefore use random data.

These numbers also settle the choice of backend. Following the per-bit argument of \[20, §3.3\], one INT8 product contributes ≈7.85 bits to log<sub>2</sub>_M_ at 186TOP/s, whereas one DGEMM in an FP64-based Ozaki-II backend contributes ≈21.5 bits (_k_=4096) at 0.76 TFLOP/s. Per bit of accuracy, the INT8 path is thus ≈90 times cheaper on this device, and we do not consider an FP64 backend.

## 4 The emulation algorithm as implemented

Algorithm 1 summarizes the pipeline for one output tile; in the common case the whole matrix _C_ forms a single tile. All steps run on the GPU, and the host only computes tables of size _O(s_). In the following we describe each step and indicate where it follows the literature and where it departs from it.

### 4.1 Choice of the scaling width _t_

For _x\>_0 let e(_x_) denote the binary exponent returned by the C function `frepxp`, i.e. the integer with \(2^{\mathrm{e}(x)-1}\le x<2^{\mathrm{e}(x)}\). The scaling exponents in Eq. (1) are<tbc>

\(D_i=t-\mathrm{e}\big(\mathrm{max}_p|a_{ip}|\big),E_j=t-\mathrm{e}\big(\mathrm{max}_p|b_{pj}|\big),\) (3)

<tbc>so that |_a<sub>ip</sub>_2<sup>_D<sub>i</sub>_</sup>|_\<_2_<sup>t</sup>_ and, after rounding, \(|\hat{a}_{ip}|\le 2^t\) (likewise for _B_). To choose _t_, we impose the a-priori bound

\(|\hat{c}_{ij}|\le k2^{2t}\le M/4,\) (4)

which is half of the range required for uniqueness in Eq. (2). This factor of 1/2 is the price of the fast quotient evaluation described in Section 4.4; it costs one bit of _t_ per two moduli.  2 lists _t_ for typical values of _k_. For \(s\ge 16\) and \(k\le 2^{14}\) we have \(t\ge 53\), so every element within _t_-53 binades of its row maximum is represented exactly.

## 4.3 INT8 products

The _s_ products are issued as a single strided-batch call (`oneapi::mkl::blas::gemm\_batch`, `int8`\(\times\)`int8`\(\rightarrow\)`int32`). For _k\>_131071 we split the _k_ dimension into chunks and sum their residues in the reconstruction.

## 4.4 CRT reconstruction with an FP32 quotient

Let \(r_t\in[0,2m_t)\) be any representative of \(C_{ij}^{(t)}\) mod _m<sub>t</sub>_ and _W<sub>t</sub>=M<sub>t</sub>y<sub>t</sub>_. Then \(Z=\sum_tr_tW_t\equiv\hat{c}_{ij}\) (mod _M_) and, exactly,

\(\frac{Z}{M}=\sum_{t=1}^s\frac{r_ty_t}{m_t},\) (6)

an identity also used in \[20, §4.4\]. Writing \(Z=\hat{c}_{ij}+qM\) with \(q\in\mathbb{Z}\), the bound of Eq. (4) gives \(|Z/M-q|\le 1/4\). The integer _q_ can therefore be recovered from a crude approximation of _Z/M_.

**Lemma 1.** _Let_ \(\tilde{z}\) _be_ \(\sum_tr_t\text{fl}_{32}(y_t/m_t)\) _accumulated with s FP32 fused multiply-ads. For_ \(s\le 24\) _and_ \(m_t\le 256\), \(|\tilde{z}-Z/M|<2^{-6}\)_; hence_ \(q=\text{rint}(\tilde{z})\).

_Proof sketch._ All partial sums are below \(2\cdot 256\cdot 24<2^{14}\), so each FMA contributes a rounding error of at most 2<sup>-11</sup>, and each representation error satisfies \(|r_t(\text{fl}_{32}(y_t/m_t)-y_t/m_t)|\le 2^92^{-24}\). The total is below 24(2<sup>-11</sup>+2<sup>-15</sup>)_\<_2<sup>-6</sup>, well inside the margin of 1/4.

**Algorithm 3** CRT kernel (one work-item per entry (_i,j_))

3: \(r\leftarrow\text{Barrett}(C_{ij}^{(t)}+2^{31})+K'_t\triangleright r\in[0,2m_t)\), \(K'_t=(-2^{31})\mathrm{mod}m_t\)

4: \(\tilde{z}\leftarrow\text{fma}_{32}(r,y_t/m_t,\tilde{z})\)

5: \(acc_\ell\leftarrow acc_\ell+r\cdot W_{t,\ell}\) for all \(\ell\triangleright 16\)-bit limbs of _W<sub>t</sub>=M<sub>t</sub>y<sub>t</sub>_

6: **end for**

7: \(q\leftarrow\text{rint}(\tilde{z})\); \(acc_\ell\leftarrow acc_\ell-qM_\ell\); propagate carries \(\triangleright\hat{c}=Z-qM\) exactly

8: \(c\leftarrow\text{RoundToDouble}(\hat{c})\cdot 2^{-D_i-E_j}\triangleright\) normalize, sticky bit, RNE

9: \(C_{ij}\leftarrow\alpha c+\beta C_{ij}\)

Once _q_ is known, \(\hat{c}_{ij}=Z-qM\) is an integer with \(|\hat{c}_{ij}|\le M/4<2^{32N_L-1}\), where \(N_L=\lfloor\mathrm{log}_2M/32\rfloor+1\), and we compute it exactly in two’s complement modulo 2<sup>32_N<sub>L</sub>_</sup>. Neither long division nor correction steps are needed, in contrast with the FP64 quotient estimate and subsequent integer correction of \[17, 20\]. We accumulate _Z_ in 16-bit limbs held in 32-bit registers. Every term satisfies \(r_t\cdot W_{t,\ell}<2^9\cdot 2^{16}\), and 24 such terms stay below 2<sup>30</sup>, so carries need to be propagated only once at the end; moreover, all multiplications are \(16\times 16\)-bit, which Xe2 executes natively, unlike \(32\times 32\rightarrow 64\)-bit products. Finally, the 32_N<sub>L</sub>_-bit integer is normalized, its top 64 bits are OR-ed with a sticky bit of the remaining bits and converted with round-to- nearest-even, and the result is multiplied by the exact power of two 2<sup>-_D<sub>i</sub>-E<sub>j</sub>_</sup>. The output is therefore the correctly rounded value of \(2^{-D_i-E_j}\hat{c}_{ij}\) unless it is subnormal.

### 4.5 Error bound and the precision knob

Combining the rounding in Eq. (1) with the final rounding gives, for every entry,

\(|\tilde{c}_{ij}-c_{ij}|\le\frac{1}{2}2^{-D_i}\sum_p|b_{pj}|+\frac{1}{2}2^{-E_j}\sum_p|a_{ip}|+\frac{1}{4}k2^{-D_i-E_j}+u|\tilde{c}_{ij}|,\) (7)

which our tests verify element by element (Section 8.1). Since 2<sup>-_D<sub>i</sub>_</sup>≈2<sup>-_t_</sup>max_<sub>p</sub>|a<sub>ip</sub>_|, the first three terms are of order 2<sup>-_t_</sup>(|_A_||_B_|)_<sub>ij</sub>_. The number of moduli _s_ thus determines _t_ and, through it, the accuracy. The helper `moduli\_for\_bits`(_k,b_) returns the smallest _s_ for which \(t\ge b\).

## 5 Complex matrix multiplication (ZGEMM)

For _A=A<sub>r</sub>+iA<sub>i</sub>_ and _B=B<sub>r</sub>+iB<sub>i</sub>_ we use one shared exponent per row of op(_A_), taken over both real and imaginary parts, and one per column of op(_B_). The integrated parts then satisfy \(|\mathrm{Re}\hat{C}|,|\mathrm{Im}\hat{C}|\le 2k2^{2t}\), so _t_ is chosen with 2_k_ in place of _k_ in Eq. (4). As in \[19\], we use the 3M (Karatsuba) form

\(P_0=\hat{A}_r\hat{B}_r,P_1=\hat{A}_i\hat{B}_i,P_2=(\hat{A}_r+\hat{A}_i)(\hat{B}_r+\hat{B}_i),\mathrm{Re}\hat{C}=P_0-P_1,\mathrm{Im}\hat{C}=P_2-P_0-P_1,\) (8)

evaluated entirely in residues. The split kernel emits three groups of _s_ planes, \(\mathrm{sym}(\hat{a}_r)\), \(\mathrm{sym}(\hat{a}_i)\) and \(\mathrm{sym}(\mathrm{sym}(\hat{a}_r)+\mathrm{sym}(\hat{a}_i))\), and implements conjugation by negating the imaginary residue. Three strided-batch INT8 GEMMs follow, and the CRT kernel forms (_P_<sub>0</sub>-_P_<sub>1</sub>) mod_m<sub>t</sub>_ and (_P_<sub>2</sub>-_P_<sub>0</sub>-_P_<sub>1</sub>) mod_m<sub>t</sub>_ before two independent reconstructions. Because every product is exact, the 3M form incurs no accuracy penalty here, unlike its floating-point counterpart \[31\], and it saves a quarter of the INT8 GEMMs (3_s_ instead of 4_s_). Algorithm 4 summarizes the procedure.

1: \(t\leftarrow\) Eq. (4) with 2_k_; _D<sub>i</sub>,E<sub>j</sub>_ from max(|Re|,|Im|)

## 6 Implementation decisions specific to Intel Arc (Xe2)

### Kernel code generation.

The split and CRT kernels are templates over _s_. All loops over moduli are unrolled, and the modulus tables (at most 1KB) are passed as kernel arguments instead of being read from memory. Both kernels use sub-groups of 32 work-items; the complex split uses 16 because of register pressure. With integer-only residue generation, 16-bit limbs and a \[0,2_m_) representative, both kernels are memory-bound: at _N_=8192 the split kernel streams 270-340GB/s and the CRT kernel 373-416GB/s, i.e. close to the measured memory bandwidth ( 3).

### Using the vendor INT8 GEMM.

The INT8 products are computed by the batched GEMM of oneMKL (`gemm\_batch`), which reaches 184-193TOP/s on the B60. A hand-written `joint\_matrix` kernel is possible, but offers no advantage: the INT8 GEMM is currently a core operation of the vendor’s inference stack and is tuned by the vendor for each generation of XMX engines. Relying on it lets the emulation inherit these improvements without changes to our code, and confines our own kernels to the memory-bound split and CRT phases. We do, however, adapt the calling pattern to three behaviours of the routine that we measured: (i) with `transb=trans` its throughput drops from 175 to 33TOP/s, so we first transpose a transposed op(_B_) through shared local memory into a temporary tile and always store the residue planes of _B_ in `N` layout; (ii) a leading dimension of the _A_ planes that is a multiple of \(12288=3\cdot 4096\) reduces the throughput to 120-145TOP/s, which a padding of 64 bytes eliminates ( 4); (iii) tiles whose row count is not a power of two run 5-17% slower, so the tiler prefers _m<sub>b</sub>_=2_<sup>j</sup>_ (Figure 1).

### Memory-aware tiling.

A tile of size \(m_b\times n_b\) requires a workspace of _s(m<sub>b</sub>k+kn<sub>b</sub>_+4_m<sub>b</sub>n<sub>b</sub>_) bytes (\(\times 3\) for ZGEMM). When this exceeds the memory budget, _C_ is tiled. Candidate tile sizes are scored with a simple cost model, consisting of the GEMM time with a shape-efficiency factor plus the split and CRT traffic, and the cheapest feasible tiling is selected. ## 8 Results

### 8.1 Correctness

The test program (108 tests) checks the bound of Eq. (7) element-wise against the double-double reference for all combinations of `N/T/C`, \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), leading dimensions larger than the row count, _s_=2..24, _k_ from 1 to 300000, and tiling under a workspace limit of 4-8MB; tiled results are bitwise identical to untiled ones. Two unit tests follow \[20\]. The split kernel is compared with `\_int128` arithmetic on 2.2 million residues, including subnormals and signed zeros, and the CRT kernel reconstructs 8192 random exact integers with \(|\hat{c}|\le M/4\) (including \(|\hat{c}|=M/4\)) for every _s_=2..24. Both tests report zero mismatches. Integer inputs give bitwise exact results, and Inf/NaN inputs propagate NaN to the affected row or column.

### 8.2 Accuracy

Figure 2 and  6 show how the error depends on _s_. The componentwise error decreases by a factor of about 2<sup>4</sup> per modulus, as predicted by _t_≈(log<sub>2</sub>_M_-log<sub>2</sub>_k)/_2. The componentwise accuracy of native DGEMM is reached at _s_=14-15 for well-scaled data and at _s_=17 for \(\phi=2\) ( 7). Beyond this point the result becomes correctly rounded. For U\[-1,1), all entries are correctly rounded from _s_=15-16 on, whereas native DGEMM rounds only 1.7-3% (oneMKL on the GPU) and 2-13% (MKL on the CPU) of the entries correctly, with maximum errors of 10<sup>5</sup>-10<sup>7</sup> ulps caused by cancellation. For inputs with wide exponent ranges (\(\phi=0.5\)-2 and sin/cos), correct rounding requires _t\>_62 and thus the extended-width path with _s_=19-23.

### 8.3 Worst cases

8 collects inputs designed to stress the method.

_Boundary of the CRT range._ If all entries equal 1-2<sup>-53</sup>, they round to \(\hat{a}=2^t\) and give \(|\hat{c}|=k2^{2t}=M/4\), the limit of Eq. (4). The results are exact for all _s_.

_Spike._ One element per row of _A_ is 2<sup>40</sup> times larger than the others. The shared row exponent then leaves the remaining elements only _t_-40 bits, and at _s_=16 the componentwise error is 10<sup>-10</sup>, four orders of magnitude worse than DGEMM. Increasing _s_ to 20 restores DGEMM- level accuracy, and _s_=24 gives correct rounding. This is the fundamental limitation of all shared-exponent schemes.

_Cancellation._ With _A_=\[_XX_\] and _B_=\[_Y_;-_Y_+2<sup>-30</sup>_Z_\] we obtain |_C_|≈2<sup>-30</sup>|_A_||_B_|. Native DGEMM loses 30 bits (normwise relative error \(2\times 10^{-6}\) on the GPU and \(7\times 10^{-7}\) on the CPU). Ozaki scheme II with \(s\ge 20\), in contrast, represents the inputs exactly, computes \(\hat{c}\) exactly and rounds only once: the normwise error is \(9\times 10^{-16}\) at _s_=20, and the result is correctly rounded at _s_=24.

## 8.4 DGEMM performance

9 and Figure 3 report the emulated rate for square problems. For \(N\ge 2048\) the emulation outperforms native DGEMM for every _s_. At _N_=8192 it reaches 17.3, 12.1 and 9.3 TFLOP/s for _s_=8, 12 and 16, which is 22.8, 15.9 and 12.2 times the native DGEMM rate (0.76 TFLOP/s). Problems up to _N_=24576 are tiled automatically (24576<sup>3</sup> requires ≈9GB of workspace in addition to the 14.5GB occupied by _A_, _B_ and _C_) at an efficiency loss of 0-10%. For \(N\le 256\), kernel-launch overheads (≈0.15ms) dominate, and native DGEMM is faster. Non-square shapes ( 10) behave as the operation count predicts: a small inner dimension (_k_=256) leaves the memory-bound phases exposed (2.4 TFLOP/s at _s_=8), whereas a large one approaches the GEMM bound (19.6 TFLOP/s for _k_=32768). ## 9 Discussion

### 9.1 Using the library as a BLAS replacement

The interface mirrors `dgemm` and `zgemm` of the oneMKL SYCL API with a single extra argument, the number of moduli. We recommend the following policy. By default we take _s_=`moduli\_for\_bits`(_k,_53), i.e. _s_=15-16 for \(k\le 2^{16}\); this is as accurate as DGEMM for well-scaled data and correctly rounded for U\[-1,1). Inputs with wide exponent ranges, or computations in which cancellation is expected, call for _s_=20-24, while _s_=8-12 suffices where an accuracy between FP32 and FP64 is acceptable. Because all accumulation is performed in exact integer arithmetic, the results are deterministic and independent of the tiling. Existing applications currently have to call the library explicitly; a layer that transparently redirects their oneMKL calls is left for future work.

### 9.2 Performance model and outlook to Xe3/Xe3P

The measured run time is well described by

\(T\approx\frac{2mnksg}{R_8}+\frac{g\big[(16+s)(mk+kn)+(4s+8)mn\big]}{\beta_\text{mem}}+n_\text{launch}\tau,\) (9)

where _g_=1 for DGEMM and _g_=3 for ZGEMM, _R_<sub>8</sub> is the INT8 GEMM rate, \(\beta_\text{mem}\) the memory bandwidth and \(\tau\approx 15\mu\)s the launch overhead. The three terms correspond to the three kinds of work in the pipeline. The first is the time of the _s_ INT8 products of 2_mnk_ operations each. The second is the memory traffic of the remaining kernels, in bytes: the scaling and split kernels read every element of _A_ and _B_ twice as FP64 (16 bytes) and write _s_ residue bytes, and the CRT kernel reads _s_ INT32 products (4_s_ bytes) and writes one FP64 result (8 bytes) per entry of _C_. The third counts the kernel launches. With the B60 values of  1, the model matches the measurements to within 10% on average and to within 1-8% for \(4096\le N\le 8192\) ( 17). It underestimates the time for small problems, where the INT8 GEMM runs below its asymptotic rate, and for _N_=12288, where oneMKL is slower for this shape. ### 9.3 Limitations

• Exponents are shared per row and column, so elements more than _t_-53 binades below the row maximum lose bits (Section 8.3); a larger _s_ mitigates this.<tbc>

• The number of moduli is limited to \(s\le 24\) (log<sub>2</sub>_M\<_192); _k\>_131071 is handled by splitting _k_.<tbc>

• An Inf or NaN in a row of op(_A_) or a column of op(_B_) produces NaN in the entire corresponding row or column of _C_, and subnormal results may be double-rounded.<tbc>

• The workspace grows as _s(mk+kn_+4_mn_) bytes (\(\times 3\) for ZGEMM). Large problems are tiled, at the cost of re-splitting parts of _A_.<tbc>

• Small problems (\(N\lesssim 256\)) are dominated by launch overhead.
